quiz.name: MDC-301 W1 — Polynomial and Regularised Regression

questions.question: Why is polynomial regression called linear in its parameters even when its curve bends?
options: The fitted curve is always a straight line
The transformed features are combined as a linear weighted sum of coefficients
It uses no powers of x
questions.explanation: A basis such as [1, x, x²] can curve with x while the coefficients still enter linearly.

questions.question: For unregularised OLS fitted on the same rows, what is true when a higher-degree polynomial adds nested features?
options: Training squared error cannot increase, though test error may worsen
questions.explanation: The expanded model can reproduce the lower-degree model by setting new coefficients to zero; better training fit does not ensure better generalisation.

questions.question: Why is training error alone a poor way to choose polynomial degree?
options: A more flexible model can fit training rows more closely but generalise worse
Higher degree always reduces test error
questions.explanation: Choose complexity using validation evidence and reserve the test set for the final evaluation.

questions.question: Where should PolynomialFeatures normally sit during a train/validation workflow?
options: As part of a pipeline fitted within the training split or fold
Outside the workflow after inspecting test labels
Only after the regression model predicts
It cannot be used before a linear model
questions.explanation: A pipeline keeps feature construction and the predictor together during splitting and cross-validation. PolynomialFeatures itself is a deterministic map, but the pipeline helps ensure consistent workflow.

questions.question: For one input x = 3 and degree 2, what row does PolynomialFeatures(include_bias=True) produce?
questions.explanation: With the bias term, the one-feature degree-2 basis is [1, x, x²].

questions.question: Which penalty does Ridge regression add to the squared-error objective?
options: L1: a sum of absolute coefficient values
L2: a sum of squared coefficient values
questions.explanation: Ridge uses an L2 penalty that discourages large coefficients.

questions.question: What is a characteristic effect of Lasso's L1 penalty?
options: It can set some fitted coefficients exactly to zero
It guarantees every coefficient is positive
It forces every coefficient to be equal
It removes the need for a test set
questions.explanation: The L1 penalty can produce sparse coefficient vectors, although feature scaling and the penalty value matter.

questions.question: If X contains predictors only and the intercept is handled separately, what is the Ridge coefficient solution for penalty λ > 0?
questions.explanation: Differentiating ||y − Xβ||² + λ||β||² gives (XᵀX + λI)β̂ = Xᵀy.

questions.question: As Ridge penalty strength λ becomes very large, what generally happens to the penalised feature coefficients?
questions.explanation: A stronger L2 penalty pulls feature coefficients toward zero; a separately handled intercept is not penalised in this formulation.

questions.question: ElasticNet combines which two regularisation penalties?
questions.explanation: ElasticNet combines L1 and L2 penalties, joining some Lasso and Ridge behaviours.
